[Assistant]: For a set of pirates let $V$ be the set of pirates and let $E$ be the set of
mutual gun-points.  Put $v=|V|=9$.  The hypothesis that no two bullets
cross is the hypothesis that the graph $G=(V,E)$ can be drawn in the
plane without crossings.  The hypothesis that the pirates do not split
into isolated groups is the hypothesis that $G$ is connected.  For a
connected plane graph

$$v-e+f=2\tag{1}$$

where $f$ is the number of (closed) faces of the drawing, the outer
unbounded face included.  Hence with $e=16$

$$f=2-v+e=2-9+16=9$$

is the number of faces of any plane drawing of the configuration.  In
particular every face is bounded by a closed walk in $G$ and in a simple
drawing the walk can be taken to be a simple cycle.  In the language of
the problem a simple cycle is a (minimal) Mexican standoff: every pirate
on the cycle is pointing at the next pirate on the cycle and is pointed
at by the previous one.  Hence, up to the choice of the embedding, the
minimal standoffs are in $1\!-\!1$ correspondence with the faces of the
embedding.

Now
$\sum_{F} |F|=2e$, the sum being over the $f$ faces counted with
multiplicity, so that with $f_{k}$ the number of faces of length $k$,

$$\sum_{k\ge 3}k\,f_{k}=2e=32,\qquad\sum_{k\ge 3}f_{k}=f=9 .
\tag{2}$$

In particular every face has $|F|\ge 3$, otherwise two vertices would be
joined by two distinct edges.  The nine faces are the nine distinct
minimal standoffs which can be realised in the drawing.  Discarding the
unbounded outer face there are $f-1=8$ interior standoffs.  In the
usual counting the outer face is also a standoff, so that the drawing
can contain at most

$$f=2-v+e=9$$

distinct face–standoffs, i.e. eight proper interior standoffs, of
length $\ge3$.  This is the Euler bound; it is attained e.g. by any
connected plane graph with $v=9$, $e=16$.  If the outer face is not
counted the maximal number of interior Mexican standoffs is $f-1=8$,
often quoted as the nine faces of the planar embedding.

*Remark.*  With the usual convention of counting only interior faces the
maximal number of interior standoffs is $8$.  The nine faces counted with
the outer face is the Euler number $f=9$.

[Assistant]: For the transpositions $(i\;i+p)$ and $(i\;i+q)$ let

$$G_{n}(p,q)=\{i\sim j\;:\;|i-j|\in\{p,q\},\;1\le i,j\le n\}$$

and put $a=\min \{p,q\}$, $b=\max \{p,q\}$, $(a,b)=1$.
A product of the allowed transpositions is the whole alternating group
iff $G_{n}(p,q)$ is connected and in that case the transpositions
$(i\;i+a)$ and $(i\;i+b)$ generate $S_{n}$.  Put $r\equiv a\pmod a$.
The $a$--edges join the $a$ residue classes mod $a$, a $b$--edge joins
the two classes $r$ and $r+b\pmod a$.  Hence on the residue graph the
$b$--edges generate the cyclic group ${\mathbf Z}/a{\mathbf Z}$ and the
whole graph is connected iff a $b$--edge can be used to join the two
extreme residue classes.  The first $b$--edge which can be used is
$1\mapsto 1+b$ and the last one which can be used is $n-b\mapsto n$.
Hence the $a$-- and $b$--edges meet iff

$$1+b\le n-a+1\iff a+b\le n+1, $$

and then every cut $k\mid 1\le k<n$ is crossed by an $a$-- or a
$b$--edge.  In particular $a\le n/2$ and, with $(a,b)=1$,

$$G_{n}(p,q)\ {\rm is\ connected}\iff a+b\le n+1\iff p+q\le n+1,$$

and for $(p,q)=1$ this is also sufficient.  Up to order we may write
$p<q$; then

$$ (p,q)\ {\rm good}\iff (p,q)=1,\;p>1,\;q>1,\;p+q\le n+1,
\tag{*}$$

and for coprime $p,q>1$ this is $p+q\le n+1$, i.e. $n\ge p+q-1$,
which is the familiar Frobenius condition.  In particular $a\le n/2$ is
necessary and $p+q=n+1$ is the extremal good case.

Denote by $N_{n}$ the number of ordered pairs $2\le p,q\le n$ with
$(p,q)=1$ and $p+q\le n+1$.  For $2\le p\le n-1$

$$\#\{q:2\le q\le n+1-p\} = n-p, $$

hence

$$N_{n}^{\;0}:=\#\{p,q\ge2:p+q\le n+1\}
      =\sum_{p=2}^{\,n-1}(n-p)=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}2 ,$$

and $N_{n}^{0}/(n-1)^{2}\to 1/2$.  Let $C_{n}$ be the number of
coprime pairs in this triangle.  By the usual equidistribution of
$\gcd$,

$$\frac{C_{n}}{N_{n}^{0}}\longrightarrow
\frac{6}{\pi^{2}},\qquad n\to\infty, $$

the $6/\pi^{2}$ being the density of coprime pairs in ${\mathbf N}^{2}$.
Hence with the usual normalisation for ordered pairs
$2\le p,q\le n$

$$ \Pr_{n}:=\frac{C_{n}}{(n-1)^{2}}
       =\frac{N_{n}^{0}}{(n-1)^{2}}\;\frac{C_{n}}{N_{n}^{0}}
       \longrightarrow \frac12\frac{6}{\pi^{2}}=\frac{3}{\pi^{2}}, $$

i.e. about $0.304$ of all ordered pairs $p,q\ge2$ are good.  Up to
order the same constant is obtained.  In particular, if the pair is
already known to be coprime and $>1$,

$$ \Pr\bigl[p+q\le n+1\mid (p,q)=1\bigr]\longrightarrow\frac12,
$$

so that asymptotically one half of the coprime pairs $p,q>1$ satisfy
the Frobenius condition $p+q\le n+1$ and hence are good.  This is the
usual $1/2$ statement.  The unconditional density is $3/\pi^{2}$,
which is the $6/\pi^{2}$ coprime density multiplied by the $1/2$
triangular density. ∎
